description: How attackers break the hardware under software and how designers defend it: roots of trust, secure boot, side channels, fault injection, trusted execution and physical tampering. Students attack and harden simulated microcontrollers, sensors and IoT nodes on the hardware bench.
modelledOn: Anderson, Security Engineering (chapters on tamper resistance and side channels)
Mangard, Oswald and Popp, Power Analysis Attacks
Arm Platform Security Architecture (PSA Certified) threat models
ETSI EN 303 645 consumer IoT security baseline
outcomes: Build a threat model for an embedded device that states attacker capabilities, assets and the attack surface.
Design and verify a secure boot chain with signed firmware, rollback protection and locked debug ports.
Carry out timing and power-analysis attacks on simulated traces and recover key material, then apply masking or constant-time countermeasures.
Explain how glitching and other fault attacks bypass checks and select countermeasures that detect or tolerate faults.
Partition a system between trusted and untrusted worlds and assess the limits of trusted execution environments.
Secure an IoT sensor network end to end, covering identity, communication, updates and data integrity.

units.title: Threat models and the hardware attack surface
topics: Adversary models: remote, local and physical attackers, their budgets and skills
Anatomy of an embedded device: microcontroller, flash, SRAM, peripherals, buses and debug ports
Supply chain threats: counterfeit chips, hardware trojans and tampered firmware at the factory
Security evaluation schemes: Common Criteria, FIPS 140-3 and PSA Certified levels
Case studies: prepaid electricity meters, smart-card payment terminals and point-of-sale devices in Ghana

units.title: Hardware root of trust
topics: Immutable boot ROM, one-time-programmable fuses and device identity
Secure elements and the TPM 2.0: platform configuration registers, measured boot and remote attestation
Key storage and provisioning; hardware key hierarchies; physically unclonable functions
True random number generators: entropy sources, conditioning and health tests
Cryptographic accelerators and constant-time engines

units.title: Secure boot and firmware integrity
topics: Chain of trust from ROM to bootloader to operating system with ECDSA or RSA signature checks
Secure firmware update: signed images, rollback protection, A/B partitions and over-the-air delivery
Firmware analysis: dumping flash, unpacking images, string and entropy analysis, finding hard-coded keys
Debug interface risks: JTAG, SWD and UART; lock bits and debug authentication
Memory protection on microcontrollers: MPU, stack canaries, W^X and return-oriented attacks on embedded code

units.title: Side-channel attacks
topics: Timing attacks on password comparison, RSA exponentiation and table-lookup AES; constant-time coding
Simple power analysis of square-and-multiply and PIN verification
Differential and correlation power analysis of the AES first round with the Hamming-weight model
Cache attacks (Prime+Probe, Flush+Reload) and transient execution attacks (Spectre, Meltdown)
Electromagnetic and acoustic leakage; countermeasures: masking, hiding and shuffling

units.title: Fault injection
topics: Fault methods: voltage and clock glitching, electromagnetic and laser fault injection
Fault effects: skipped instructions, corrupted branches and bypassing a secure boot check
Differential fault analysis of AES and the Bellcore attack on RSA-CRT
Rowhammer and other memory fault attacks
Countermeasures: redundant computation, double checks, glitch sensors and error-detecting codes

units.title: Trusted execution environments
topics: Arm TrustZone: secure and non-secure worlds, secure monitor calls and memory partitioning
Enclaves and confidential computing: Intel SGX, AMD SEV and remote attestation
Attacks on TEEs: controlled-channel, transient execution and interface bugs
Memory encryption, integrity trees and hardware isolation with RISC-V PMP and capability hardware (CHERI)
Partitioning a design: what belongs in the trusted world, minimising the trusted computing base

units.title: Physical and tamper attacks
topics: Tamper resistance, evidence, detection and response: meshes, sensors, potting and key zeroisation
Invasive and semi-invasive attacks: decapsulation, microprobing and imaging
Board-level attacks: bus sniffing on SPI and I2C flash, cold-boot and PCB probing
Payment terminal and ATM skimmer attacks; PCI PTS requirements
Anti-counterfeiting: authentication tokens, secure supply chains and device cloning defences

units.title: Securing IoT devices and sensors
topics: IoT threat modelling: STRIDE on the sensor-gateway-cloud chain; OWASP IoT top ten and ETSI EN 303 645
Secure communication on constrained devices: DTLS, TLS with pre-shared keys, MQTT over TLS and LoRaWAN key management
Device identity, onboarding and credential management; default passwords and the Mirai botnet
Sensor data integrity and spoofing: GPS spoofing, ADC injection and signal-level attacks
Capstone: design and secure a solar-powered farm sensor network from chip to cloud

schedule.title: Attack surface of embedded devices
schedule.exercise: Write a one-page threat model for a prepaid electricity meter: assets, attacker types (customer, installer, remote), entry points and the three highest-risk attacks.

tasks.title: Label the flash, SRAM, UART, SPI and debug header on a virtual microcontroller board and list which ones an attacker with physical access can reach.
Rank five attacker profiles against a sensor node by required skill, cost and access, and mark which assets each can reach.
Inspect a delivered board for supply chain tampering by comparing its flash contents and chip markings with a reference, and report every deviation found.

schedule.title: Roots of trust and attestation
schedule.exercise: Draw the key hierarchy of a device with a unique fused key, a boot key and per-application keys, and explain what a cloned device would still lack.

tasks.title: Blow a simulated fuse that stores the boot public key hash and show the boot ROM rejecting an image signed by a different key.
Extend PCR registers through a three-stage measured boot and verify the final value against the expected quote.
Simulate a ring-oscillator physically unclonable function for 20 devices, measure uniqueness and reliability, and decide whether the response is usable as a key.

schedule.title: Randomness and cryptographic hardware
schedule.exercise: Explain how a weak random number generator in a key-generating device can be recovered by an attacker who sees only public keys.

tasks.title: Run the repetition-count and frequency health tests on 10000 bits from a good and a biased noise source and report which fails.
Sample the ADC noise on a virtual microcontroller, condition it with a hash and check the output passes simple randomness tests.
Compare cycle counts of a software AES using table lookups and a constant-time version, and show which one leaks the key index timing.

schedule.title: Chain of trust and firmware updates
schedule.exercise: Design the update flow for a remote weather station with an unreliable link: how images are signed, how rollback is blocked and what happens if power fails mid-update.

tasks.title: Boot a virtual board with a valid signed image, then flip one byte of the image and confirm secure boot refuses it.
Apply a signed update with a version counter, then try to install the older vulnerable image and show the rollback check blocking it.
Implement an A/B partition update that survives power loss at each of five points in the install sequence, with the device always bootable.

schedule.title: Firmware analysis and debug interfaces
schedule.exercise: Given a firmware dump from a smart plug, list the steps from extraction to finding a hard-coded credential, and propose how the vendor should have prevented it.

tasks.title: Run strings and an entropy scan on a firmware image in the terminal and locate the hard-coded Wi-Fi password.
Connect to the UART console of a virtual router board, read the boot log, find the root shell and then disable it with a lock bit.
Step through a stack overflow on a microcontroller without an MPU, then show how a stack canary and W^X stop the same exploit.

schedule.title: Timing and power analysis
schedule.exercise: Explain in words why the power consumption of an S-box output depends on the key byte, and work the correlation by hand for a four-trace toy example.

tasks.title: Recover a 4-character PIN from a comparison function by measuring its response time per guess, one character at a time.
Read a power trace of square-and-multiply modular exponentiation and recover the private exponent bits from the long and short peaks.
Run correlation power analysis on 500 simulated AES traces, plot correlation per key guess for byte 0 and recover the key byte.

schedule.title: Cache, transient and electromagnetic leakage
schedule.exercise: Describe how first-order Boolean masking removes the dependency between leaked values and the key, and why second-order attacks still work.

tasks.title: Step through a Flush+Reload probe on a shared cache line and decide from hit and miss times whether the victim accessed it.
Trace a speculative out-of-bounds read in a bounds-check bypass and identify which cache line reveals the secret byte.
Add first-order masking to the simulated AES S-box and rerun correlation power analysis to show the attack on 500 traces now fails.

schedule.title: Fault injection and countermeasures
schedule.exercise: For a signature check written as a single if statement, describe how a clock glitch could skip it, and redesign the check with redundancy.

tasks.title: Apply a voltage glitch of varying width to a virtual microcontroller and record at which widths the instruction is skipped or corrupted.
Sweep glitch offset and width against a PIN check loop to find the setting that bypasses the failed-attempt counter.
Mount the Bellcore attack on an RSA-CRT signature with one faulty output, factor the modulus with a gcd and verify the recovered primes.

schedule.title: TrustZone and enclaves
schedule.exercise: Compare TrustZone-style worlds and SGX-style enclaves in a table: what each protects, what it trusts and one real attack class against each.

tasks.title: Step a secure monitor call from the normal world into the secure world and back, noting which registers and memory regions change.
Verify a remote attestation report for a simulated enclave and reject a report whose measurement does not match the expected hash.
Observe the page-access sequence of an enclave in a controlled-channel attack and infer which branch of a secret-dependent function was taken.

schedule.title: Memory isolation and trusted computing base design
schedule.exercise: Take a smart-meter firmware with 40 modules and decide which belong in the trusted world, arguing for the smallest trusted computing base that still protects the keys and tariff logic.

tasks.title: Configure RISC-V PMP regions so user code can read the sensor buffer but not the key region, then test a violating access.
Walk a memory read through an integrity tree and show how a tampered DRAM block is detected by a hash mismatch.
Partition a smart-meter design into secure and non-secure code, move only the signing routine into the secure side, and measure the change in trusted code size.

schedule.title: Tamper resistance and physical attacks
schedule.exercise: Compare tamper-evident, tamper-resistant and tamper-responsive designs for a card payment terminal and decide which suits a rural agent kiosk with no staff on site.

tasks.title: Wire a case switch and light sensor to a virtual board and make it zeroise a stored key when the enclosure is opened.
Sniff an SPI flash read on a simulated board bus, reconstruct the transferred bytes and recover a stored token.
Investigate a card skimmer incident at a petrol station terminal, decide on evidence and containment, and score the response against a rubric.

schedule.title: IoT threat modelling, communication and identity
schedule.exercise: Apply STRIDE to a soil-moisture sensor reporting through a gateway to a cloud dashboard and list one threat and one mitigation per element.

tasks.title: Build a sensor, gateway and cloud diagram for a farm moisture node and mark the trust boundaries and data flows to protect.
Publish sensor readings over MQTT with and without TLS, capture the traffic, and show what an eavesdropper sees in each case.
Scan 50 simulated devices for default credentials, show how a Mirai-style worm spreads, then give each device a unique credential and re-scan.

schedule.title: Sensor integrity and capstone
schedule.exercise: Present the capstone design review for a solar-powered farm sensor network: threat model, root of trust, update path, protocol choices and the residual risks left.

tasks.title: Add a plausibility range check and a signed timestamp to a temperature reading and test it against an injected out-of-range value.
Spoof a soil sensor by injecting voltage on the ADC pin, detect it with a redundant second sensor, and report the detection threshold used.
Harden a five-node solar sensor network with unique device keys, signed updates, encrypted telemetry and a tamper switch, then test it against a scripted attacker.
